name: Colin Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share-farm 220 hectares with an older couple, the Ashdowns, who own the land and want to stay on it without doing the work. I bring the labour and most of the machinery, they bring the land, and we split what it makes. It's wheat, oilseed rape and about 150 store cattle I buy in as youngsters and finish over the winter. In summer I also go out baling for six neighbours, which pays for the baler and a bit more. My partner Priya does the books at the vet practice in town, and the kids, Ravi and Asha, are thirteen and nine.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weather, mostly. You can plan all you like and then it rains for nine days in August. I'll use an AI chat thing now and then to check spray rules or ask about a weather window, but I double-check everything it says. I've been caught out by a confident answer before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI Plateau. That's the forecast I'd plan around anyway. You don't bet the farm on a gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the baling I'd say to the neighbours, see, no need to buy anything clever yet. I'd tell them to keep their money for fertiliser, because that's what actually hurt us last year. I'm not one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI was never my biggest worry. Our share-farming deal is a twelve-year handshake with a man of 74, and his children have never wanted the farm. If Mr Ashdown goes and the children sell, I lose the land under everything I've built, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and use the chat tool a bit more for spray records, double-checking every answer. I'd keep saving 180 a month. And I'd finally ask Mr Ashdown, gently, over a cup of tea, whether we could put the arrangement on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the low background kind. Like a field drain you know is blocked before the rain has come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you asked for it in writing before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because asking feels like saying I don't trust him, and I do. Mr Ashdown shook my hand in his kitchen in 2014 and never once went back on a word. It's his son in the city I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would losing the land actually mean for the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the cattle for a season and sell them, and I'd have a baler and a tractor and nowhere to use them. Priya's wage would carry the mortgage for a while, not for ever. I'd be looking for a farm manager's job at 44.

say: No need to **buy anything clever** yet.
Keep your money for **fertiliser**, because that's what actually hurt us last year.
think: Our share-farming deal is **a handshake** with a 74-year-old whose children have never wanted the farm.
If they sell, I lose **everything I've built** on that land.
do: Keeps farming as he is and uses the chat tool more for **spray records**.
Asks Mr Ashdown over tea whether the deal could be **put on paper**.
feel: **A low, background unease**, like a blocked field drain before the rain comes.
S0.quote: Our share-farming deal is a twelve-year handshake with a man of 74, and his children have never wanted the farm.
fieldNote: Colin treated AI as beside the point and went straight to **the land**.

steps.text: Keep farming wheat, rape and store cattle on the Ashdowns' land
Use the chat tool for spray records, checking every answer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, checking, planning, booking. That's Priya's whole job at the vet practice, near enough. My bit's mostly the tractor seat, so the robots being slower is something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the baling I'd say farm work is safe for a while, it's the offices in town that'll feel it. I'd tell the neighbours not to rush into a shared self-driving baler just because a salesman says so. Let somebody else prove it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the first hit lands at home. My partner Priya does the books, the bills and the appointment booking at the vet practice, and that's exactly the list on your card. The practice won't sack her overnight, but I can see her going from four days to two within a year or so, and that's about a third of what we bring in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Priya in the first month and look at the vet nurse course at the college, two years part-time, which keeps her with the animals instead of the computer. I'd push savings to 250 a month to cover the fees and the dip. And I'd offer to run the neighbours' shared baler for them if they buy one, rather than lose the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady with it. Mostly anxious for Priya, who's been at that practice eleven years and is proud of her books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Priya say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya would say she's been thinking it already, because she's seen the new booking system they trialled. She'd say she's 42 and not starting again, then look up the course anyway. That's how she is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if her hours drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi's football tour in the spring, which he'd hate me for. Then the second car, because Priya wouldn't need it four days a week. The cattle feed can't be cut, so it's the family stuff that goes.

I can see her going from **four days to two**, about a third of what we bring in.

Pushes savings to **250 a month** and offers to run the neighbours' shared baler.
Drops **Ravi's football tour** and the second car if Priya's hours fall.
feel: **Anxious but steady**, more for Priya, who is proud of her books, than for himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking work in 2028. That's Priya's job, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers have got a few more years than the office people this time, and we should use them sensibly instead of panicking. At the machinery ring I'd tell the neighbours not to buy the first robot that turns up in 2031. I'd say it fairly calmly, because that's how I say most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the first hit is at home, not on the farm. Priya does the books at the vet practice, and books are exactly what the AI does in 2028. My own work is hands-on, so the cattle and the baling should hold till about 2031, but then the Ashdowns could farm the land with a robot and a computer and not need me at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the baler for two more summers and sell it in 2030, before every second-hand baler in the country hits the market at once. That's maybe 18,000 if I time it right. Priya would start looking for work at the practice that's with the animals, not the computer, maybe as a vet nurse, which needs a two-year course. We'd lift our savings to 250 a month while I've still got the baling money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. It's like seeing rain coming on the forecast when the hay's still down: you know what you've got to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Priya say about retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd grumble and then do it better than anyone. She's already the one who holds the calves for the vet when they're short-handed. Priya would be fine with blood and muck; it's the course fees that would worry her, about 3,000 a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you thought about talking to the Ashdowns?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to, early, before their kids start reading about robot farms. I'd ask Mr Ashdown for a five-year agreement in writing. A handshake was enough for twelve years, but a handshake won't stand up against a robot that works for free.

say: Farmers have **a few more years** than the office people this time, so use them sensibly.
Nobody should buy **the first robot** that turns up in 2031.
think: The first hit is at home: **Priya's books** at the vet practice are exactly what the AI does in 2028.
My farm work holds until about 2031, then the Ashdowns could **farm with a robot** and not need me.
do: Keeps the baler two more summers and **sells it in 2030** for about 18,000.
Backs Priya's move to a **vet nurse course** and raises savings to 250 a month.
Asks the Ashdowns for a **five-year written agreement**.
feel: **Anxious but steady**, like seeing rain on the forecast with the hay still down.
S2.quote: A handshake was enough for twelve years, but a handshake won't stand up against a robot that works for free.
fieldNote: Colin saw that thinking AI hits **his partner's bookkeeping** before his own hands-on work.
His answer is all about **timing**: sell the baler early and get the share-farming deal in writing.
The three years of **farm income** keep him from real alarm.

steps.text: Sell the baler in 2030 for about 18,000, before second-hand prices fall
Raise savings to 250 a month while the baling money still comes in
Help Priya pay for a two-year vet nurse course, about 3,000 a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then three more. Good. Time to watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the sensible pace, and I'd tell the neighbours we've got time to do it properly. Let the big farms try the robots first. I'd still say you don't buy version one of anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's manageable. Priya's work changes in 2031, so she'd have five years to move into the vet nursing side, and my farm work holds till 2034. The baling goes when the self-driving balers come, and I'd be 51 with the cattle and the Ashdowns' land, if their kids haven't sold it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the baler for four summers and sell it in 2033. Around year two, once robots have proven themselves on a few farms locally, I'd do a farm robot operation and repair course at the college. And I'd push savings up to 300 a month in the last two years before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. I'd have a plan written on the back of a feed invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sell the baler in 2033 and not now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's still earning. Selling the baler in a panic now would cost me maybe 12,000. Timing's half of farming, and the other half is the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ravi be doing by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi would be eighteen in 2031. He likes tinkering with the quad bike, so maybe an engineering apprenticeship. I'd want him working on the robots, not competing with them.

steps.text: Keep the baler four more summers and sell it in 2033

Raise savings to 300 a month in the two years before the robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years until a robot can bale. That's a long run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, as long as people don't waste it. In the farming group chat I'd say watch, learn, then buy together. Nothing clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd be 56 by 2039, Priya would have years to change her work, and the kids would be grown. The bigger question is the land, because Mr Ashdown is 74 now and that's a lot more certain than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch for the first couple of years and change nothing. Around year three I'd buy a share in a robot cattle feeder with two neighbours, maybe 8,000 each. And I'd start putting 60 a month into a fund for Ravi and Asha's training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A long run-up suits someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy a robot feeder at all, if your own work is safe for years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to learn it while it's my choice. I'd rather be the third person who buys a farm robot than the first, but I don't want to be the last either. The last one pays full price and learns in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the land matters more. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talk to the Ashdowns' kids about a long lease or buying a slice of the land, once they inherit. I'd want that settled before 2039. A robot can't farm land it isn't allowed on.

My advice to the neighbours is **watch, learn**, then buy the machines together.

The bigger question is **the land**, because Mr Ashdown is 74 now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Priya's job doing the books would go first, and then my baling and the share-farming deal three years after, before anything was proven. What would help is plain information about which machines actually work, and help to buy them jointly with neighbours instead of each farm going alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about the land itself. Whoever owns the land does fine, whatever AI does. People like me who just work the land are the ones in the middle.

headlineQuote: Whoever owns the land does fine, whatever AI does. People like me who just work the land are the ones in the middle.
portrait: Colin Patel, 43, **share-farms** 220 hectares of wheat, oilseed rape and store cattle, and earns extra from summer baling.
He uses AI now and then but double-checks it, and **waits for proof** before buying anything.
If AI stalls he's **uneasy**, because his whole living rests on a handshake with a 74-year-old landowner.
Under steady change he's **anxious**, since Priya's bookkeeping job is exactly the work the card names.
Fast AGI keeps him **anxious**; with five or ten years he relaxes and buys shared machines once they're proven.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his partner's bookkeeping job would go first.
His **baling and share-farming deal** would follow three years later, before any machine was proven.
whatWouldHelp: **Plain information** on which machines actually work.
Help to **buy them jointly** with neighbouring farms.
